title: The Repair Lens (rupture to restoration)
note: Watches the movie through one question: how do broken things get mended? The arc: RUPTURE (something breaks) -> ARMOR (people protect the hurt place) -> TRUTH (someone sees what really happened) -> RETURN (someone goes back instead of away) -> RESTORATION (things grow back stronger, not just fixed). Timestamps approximate, tuned for Disney+.

points.title: The rupture
points.kid: Maui took something that wasn't his — and the whole world started to hurt. What does it feel like in YOUR body when something breaks between people?

quiz.question: What happens to the world after the heart is stolen?

options.text: Nothing — it was just one small stone
options.reply: Watch the darkness spreading from island to island. Small thefts can make big cracks.

options.text: A darkness starts spreading, slowly, everywhere
options.reply: YES. That's what a rupture does — it doesn't stay where it happened. It travels.
Maui loses his hook and his sky-home — but the darkness reaches everyone, even people born a thousand years later.

points.parent: This set follows one arc through the film: rupture, armor, truth, return, restoration. Every repair story starts with a break. Tonight's game: every time someone in the movie hides a hurt or mends one, name which step you're watching.

points.title: Why Dad says no (the armor)
points.kid: Moana's dad lost his best friend to the sea when he was young. How does that old hurt show up as rules today?

quiz.question: Why does Dad REALLY forbid going past the reef?

options.reply: It looks that way from outside. But his mom just told Moana the real story — an old, old hurt.

options.text: He's still scared from the night he lost his friend
options.reply: YES. The rule is armor around an old wound. He's not protecting the island — he's protecting the boy he used to be.
Watch the end of the movie before you decide that one!

points.parent: Armor = protection that outlived its moment. Elsa's gloves and 'conceal it' rule are the same move; so is Rumi hiding her patterns. Useful distinction from our KPop Demon Hunters talks: inherited patterns come in two kinds — ones that protect (Honmoon-like) and ones that shame (Gwi-Ma-like). Dad's rule started as protection. The skill is telling which is which, not obeying or ignoring.

points.title: Maui's wound
points.kid: Maui's human parents let him go. The gods caught him and made him mighty. Which part of that story do you think he hears loudest at night?

quiz.question: Why does Maui need everyone to cheer for him?

options.reply: That's the costume. He just told Moana what's underneath it — listen again.

options.text: The cheering covers a very old hurt
options.reply: YES. He was thrown away once. Every trick since has been him earning the love he didn't get. The showing off is armor.
Moana becomes a hero in this same movie and never brags once. Bragging isn't the hero part.

points.parent: The movie hands you Maui's rupture directly: abandoned as a baby, rescued by gods, and every deed since aimed at being loved for what he DOES. That's the lantern-vs-idol line: he performs to be adored (idol) instead of lighting the way (lantern) — the Saja Boys failure mode. His hook is the armor; watch what happens when it cracks.

points.title: The hook cracks (armor wins a round)
points.kid: Maui leaves when his hook might break. What is he really protecting — the hook, or something inside?
points.parent: When armor is threatened, people run — that's this scene. Maui believes without the hook he's nothing, so risking the hook feels like risking his whole self. Worth remembering in real arguments: you can't reason with armor by attacking it. Speak to the hurt underneath instead. A small body-move for the pause: make two fists (that's armor), then slowly open them.

points.title: The truth
points.kid: Moana loses everything — the hook, Maui, almost her hope. Then she decides who she is. What are the pieces she counts up?

quiz.question: What brings Moana back from giving up?

options.text: The ocean gives her a magic weapon
options.reply: The ocean actually took the heart BACK and left her alone. No gifts this time.

options.text: She remembers everyone and everything she loves, and chooses
options.reply: YES. That's the truth step — seeing clearly what happened, what she loves, and what she still chooses. Repair starts there.

options.text: Maui comes back and saves her
options.reply: He does come back — but only AFTER she's already chosen. Her truth came first.

points.parent: Truth is the middle of every repair: not blame, just seeing clearly — this is what broke, this is what I love, this is what I choose now. Notice Gramma refuses to decide for her. Nobody can do the truth step for someone else.

points.title: Return and restoration
points.kid: Te Fiti gets her heart back — and then she gives Maui a NEW hook. Why give a gift to the one who stole from her?

quiz.question: What makes this a REAL repair, not just a fix?

options.reply: Nobody gets punished! Watch what Te Fiti does instead of punishing...

options.text: Everyone comes out stronger than before the break
options.reply: YES. Te Fiti doesn't just get repaired — she repairs MAUI, hook and all. Real repair re-equips everybody. A mended place can be stronger than an unbroken one.
The opposite — Maui says out loud what he did. Repair needs the truth said, not erased.

points.parent: The whole arc lands in two minutes: Moana RETURNS instead of running, the truth is spoken (Maui owns what he did), and restoration goes beyond rewind — Te Fiti restores the hook, repair that re-equips. Repair isn't pretending the break never happened; it's growing something new over the mended place.

points.title: Repair across a generation
points.kid: Dad chose fear for years and years. Then he chose the ocean again. Can grown-ups change too?
points.parent: The quiet proof case of the master lesson: who you are is a choice, not a fixed thing. His rupture (losing his friend) built armor (the reef rule) that lasted decades — and he still got to choose again. Feeling like Te Kā is not being Te Kā; Te Kā is a weather, not a name. Good closing question for the couch: is there anything OUR family stopped doing after a hurt, that we might choose again?
